498.title: Can a mother forget? (Isaiah 49:15–16)
498.hook: even if she did, I will not forget you: engraved on my palms
498.howItsDone: Some churches read Isaiah 49:15–16 for comfort and on Mother's Day, and Christians point to it when describing God's love with a mother's tenderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah's feast for all peoples, where God will wipe away tears from every face. Your line was tears wiped away. Who did you share a meal with? Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Three in the morning. A baby stirs in the next room, makes one small sound, and the mother is awake before she knows why. She can sleep through traffic, thunder, a neighbor's party. Not that sound. The body seems to keep listening even when the mind is off. It's about as close as everyday life gets to a love that can't forget. Now set beside it a whole people who feel completely forgotten. Far from home, their city in ruins, their prayers going nowhere. And they say so, out loud, to God.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING, ONE SMALL SOUND.`

segments.voice: This part of Isaiah speaks to the people exiled in Babylon, and Jerusalem, called Zion, is pictured as a grieving woman. She says, in the King James Bible: "The LORD hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me." It's a raw line, and the Bible lets it stand. Then God answers with a question: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Notice the picture of God. Not a king, not a judge. A nursing mother. Some readers point out that the Hebrew word for compassion is related to the word for womb, so the language itself carries a mother's body. And then the passage goes further. Even a mother's love can fail. Mothers can forget; the text admits it. God's memory is stronger than that. Then the second picture: "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands." Graven means engraved, cut in, like letters in stone. Not a note on the back of a hand that washes off. A name carved into the palm, permanent, in the one place you see every time you reach for something. Jewish readers hear these words as God's promise never to abandon Zion and its people. Christians read them that way too, and some also think of the wounds in Jesus's hands, palms that carry the mark of love. Either way, the answer to Zion's complaint isn't an argument. It's a hand, held up, with her name on it.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE GRAVEN THEE UPON THE PALMS OF MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your palms. Settle, and breathe. Open your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at them. The lines, the creases, the calluses or scars, the marks of whatever work you've done. Then think of someone whose name you'd carve there if you could. Someone you never want to forget. Picture their name in your palm. And then, if it fits, picture your own name carved in a palm you can't see, held by someone who remembers you, even on days that feel forgotten. If you pray, you can rest in the promise, I will not forget thee. If you don't, simply notice what it feels like to be held in someone's memory. The bell holds the time.
Can a mother forget? Isaiah's answer to a people who felt forgotten: even if she could, God will not, and their name is carved on God's palms.

Your line: engraved on his hands. Today, each time you notice your hands, at the sink, the keyboard, the wheel, remember one person you don't want to forget. Then tell them. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

with a question about a mother, and hands with your name carved on them.

what it means: a forgotten people complain to God, and God answers with a mother's love that's stronger than any mother's, and a name carved into the palm.

499.title: No balm in Gilead? (Jeremiah 8:18–22)
499.hook: the weeping prophet asks why his people aren't healed; later a spiritual answered, there is a balm
499.howItsDone: Christians sing the African American spiritual "There Is a Balm in Gilead," and some churches read Jeremiah 8 in services of lament and in prayers for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, can a mother forget? Isaiah's answer: a name carved into God's palms. Your line was engraved on his hands. Whose name came to mind when you looked at your hands? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Some places are known for one thing. Champagne, Florida oranges, Swiss watches. In the Bible, it's balm from Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan River. It was a fragrant resin, prized as medicine for wounds, and traders carried it to Egypt. In fact, in Genesis, the caravan that buys young Joseph from his brothers is coming from Gilead, camels loaded with balm. In the Bible's world, Gilead meant medicine. So when the prophet Jeremiah wanted to say how bad things had become, he asked a question that would sound, to his listeners, almost absurd.
screen: `SOME PLACES ARE KNOWN FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?" In other words: the medicine exists, the doctors exist, so why are my people still sick? Jeremiah has been nicknamed the weeping prophet, and this passage shows why. Just before it, he grieves: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for rescue has come and gone. And just after, he wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, so he could weep day and night. Earlier in the same chapter, Jeremiah complains that other prophets were treating the people's wound lightly, saying "Peace, peace; when there is no peace." Jeremiah won't do that. He won't paper over the wound. He'd rather weep. And look closely: in these verses it's hard to tell who's speaking. Is it Jeremiah weeping? Or God? The voices blur together, as if God's grief and the prophet's are the same tears. Long after, an African American spiritual took Jeremiah's question and turned it into an answer. The song begins, there is a balm in Gilead. Not is there. There is. In the song, the balm points to Jesus, the healer. People singing out of hard lives answered yes. Jeremiah's honest question and the spiritual's answer belong together: the tears that don't pretend, and the hope that doesn't give up.
screen: then, large: `IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who's hurting. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is hurting. Someone sick, someone grieving, someone whose wound everyone else is treating lightly. Don't rush to make it better in your head. Let yourself feel Jeremiah's question for a moment: why isn't this healed? Then picture the balm. Not a fix, just something soothing laid on a wound: rest, care, a doctor's skill, a friend's presence. Picture it reaching them. If you pray, you can pray for their healing, in your own words. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention with care, and think of one way to bring them a little balm. The bell holds the time.
No balm in Gilead? Jeremiah's question, weeping that his people stay wounded though the cure exists, later answered by a spiritual: there is a balm.
Your line: there is a balm. Today, be a little balm for one hurting person: a meal, a ride, a message, an hour of listening, without saying peace, peace. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 499 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: READING THE PROPHETS AS CHRISTIANS.`

500.title: Reading the prophets as Christians
500.hook: the church reads the prophets two ways at once: justice now and hope in Christ
500.howItsDone: In many churches, readings from the prophets are paired with Gospel readings in the lectionary, so Christians hear the prophets both as promises fulfilled in Christ and as a call to justice; many denominations ground their social ministries in passages like Isaiah 61 and Luke 4.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah's question, no balm in Gilead?, and the spiritual's answer. Your line was there is a balm. Who did you bring a little balm to? Day five hundred.

Day five hundred. Take a breath; that's a lot of days. And for the last five weeks, we've been in the prophets: a burning coal on Isaiah's lips, a potter's wheel, dry bones, a man in a fish, a king on a donkey. Here's a question you might have felt along the way. When Christians read these books, are they reading about ancient Israel, or about Jesus? Is Amos about corrupt judges eight centuries before Christ, or about today? The answer the church has usually given is: yes. All of it, at once. And the clearest place to watch that happen is a small synagogue in Nazareth, on an ordinary Sabbath.

Luke chapter four. Jesus comes home to Nazareth and goes to the synagogue on the Sabbath, as he usually did. He stands to read, and someone hands him the scroll of Isaiah. He unrolls it and finds the place: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Good news for the poor, sight for the blind, freedom for captives and the bruised. Then, in the King James Bible: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." You can feel the silence. Then he says: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." That's the first way Christians read the prophets: looking for Christ. The suffering servant, the child born, the king on a donkey: Christians see these promises coming true in Jesus. But look at what Isaiah's words actually promise. Food for the poor. Freedom. Healing. Those aren't only spiritual ideas. And so the second way Christians read the prophets: as a call to justice, right now. Amos's river, Micah's three things, Jeremiah's tears. Churches that run soup kitchens and churches that write commentaries on fulfillment are often reading the same pages. Different churches lean on one way more than the other, and many hold both. And one thing worth saying plainly: these books were Israel's first. Jews have read the prophets for millennia, in their own way, and still do. Christians read them as Jesus did, as a Jew in a synagogue, with a scroll in his hands.
screen: `HE SAT DOWN, AND EVERY EYE WAITED.`
then, large: `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Luke 4:16 to 21. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it and read those six verses slowly. If not, just listen again in your head: good news to the poor, healing for the brokenhearted, freedom for captives, sight for the blind. Settle, and breathe. Now picture the synagogue, the scroll rolled up, every eye on him. Then ask yourself one question: where in my town are the poor, the captives, the bruised? And where, in my own life, do I need good news today? Hold both. If you pray, you can read the verses as a prayer. If you don't, simply let the words sit. The bell holds the time.
Reading the prophets as Christians. Two ways at once: looking for Christ in the promises, and hearing their call to justice right now.
screen: `READING THE PROPHETS AS CHRISTIANS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today it is fulfilled. Today, look for one small way the promise can come true near you: a meal for someone poor, a visit to someone stuck, a word that frees. Day five hundred.

501.title: Block close: the voices
501.hook: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a donkey king
501.howItsDone: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many people keep a single line from them, on a card, a wall or in memory, as a word to live by.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the prophets as Christians, two ways at once, and Jesus with the scroll in Nazareth. Your line was today it is fulfilled. Where did you see the promise come true, even a little? Day five hundred one.

Isaiah's lips are still stinging from a burning coal. Jeremiah, who said he was too young, has clay from the potter's house on his sleeves. Ezekiel has stood in a valley of dry bones and heard them rattle together. Daniel is fresh from the lions. Amos is still in his herdsman's clothes. Jonah is off in a corner, sulking. Hosea is talking about his children. Zechariah is describing a king on a donkey. Habakkuk argued with God and came down singing. All in one room: loud, strange, brave, often unwelcome. For weeks we've listened to them one at a time. Today, before we turn the page, we listen once more, all together.

The Hebrew word for prophet is navi, and the Bible itself shows what the job is. When Moses protests that he can't speak well, God tells him his brother Aaron will be his prophet: Aaron will say what Moses gives him to say. Not a fortune teller. A spokesperson. And look at what they spoke out about. To kings: you're not above the law. To festival crowds: your songs are noise while the poor are sold for a pair of shoes. To exiles in Babylon: comfort, you are mine, I have carved your name on my palms. To a people living in rubble: consider your ways, and build. To the hopeless: these bones can live; your old men shall dream dreams. Two notes, over and over. Warning and comfort. Justice and hope. Here's the other thing several of them share: they pushed back on the job. Like Moses before them, some argued. Jeremiah said he was only a child. Jonah paid his fare on a ship going the other way. Amos told a priest he was no prophet, just a herdsman taken from following the flock. Isaiah does say here am I, send me, but only after a coal has touched his lips. They spoke anyway. Jeremiah said that when he tried to keep quiet, the word was like a fire shut up in his bones. Christians hear the prophets pointing forward to Jesus, the one who read their scroll in Nazareth and said today. Some also hear them pointing outward, to every place where a hard truth still needs saying. Tomorrow a new block begins: we'll read the Gospel of Luke from the very first line. And the first voices in it will sound a lot like the prophets: an old priest, a young woman, a song about the hungry filled.
screen: `A FIRE SHUT UP IN THE BONES.`
then, large: `SOMEONE HAS TO SAY IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one prophet's line to keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the lines drift past. Here am I, send me. Comfort ye my people. They shall mount up with wings as eagles. I have called thee by thy name. Let judgment run down as waters. Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Not by might, nor by power. Yet I will rejoice. Is there no balm in Gilead? Notice if one of them stays with you a little longer than the rest. Don't overthink it. Then say that one a few times, slowly, until you know it by heart. If you pray, you can offer it back to God. If you don't, simply keep it. The bell holds the time.
Block close. Weeks of prophets, from Isaiah's coal to Jeremiah's balm: often reluctant messengers with two notes, warning and comfort, justice and hope.
Your line: someone has to say it. Today, keep your prophet's line close, and if a true and kind thing needs saying, say it, gently and clearly. Day five hundred one.

502.title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
502.hook: Luke, a careful researcher, writes to Theophilus, friend of God
502.howItsDone: Some Christians read a Gospel straight through, a chapter a day, and churches following the common lectionary read mainly from Luke in one year of their three-year cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close: all the prophets' voices in one room. Your line was someone has to say it. Which prophet's line did you keep? Day five hundred two, and a new block begins.

For the next ninety days, we're going to do something simple and rare. We're going to read one Gospel, Luke, from beginning to end, in order. Not jumping to the famous bits. The whole thing. And Luke starts in a way none of the other Gospels do. Mark begins with a shout in the wilderness. John begins in eternity: in the beginning was the Word. Matthew begins with a family tree. Luke begins like a careful researcher writing a cover letter. He tells you how he did his work, where his material came from, and why he's writing. Four verses, and you can almost hear him tapping his notes into a neat pile.

Here's how it opens, in the King James Bible: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." Luke admits up front that others have written about Jesus already. He's not the first. Then he describes his sources: those "which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." He's gathered what the eyewitnesses passed on. Then his method: having followed everything closely from the very first, he'll write it in order. And his purpose: "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed." Notice who he's writing to. Most excellent Theophilus. Nobody knows for sure who Theophilus was. Most excellent is the same title the book of Acts gives a Roman governor, Felix, so Theophilus may have been a person of rank. But his name means friend of God, or loved by God, and some readers have wondered whether Luke means every reader who loves God. Either way, Luke wrote him a second volume too: the book of Acts opens with his name again. Who was Luke? The Gospel never names its author. Early Christian tradition says it was Luke, a physician and a traveling companion of Paul, and the letter to the Colossians, under Paul's name, mentions Luke, the beloved physician. Some hold that tradition firmly; others weigh it differently. What the text itself shows is the method. In the King James words, he writes as one "having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first." Luke wants Theophilus to know this isn't rumor. He says he followed it all from the start.
screen: then, large: `THAT THOU MIGHTEST KNOW THE CERTAINTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write something down carefully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that has happened to you that you don't want to lose. A conversation, a moment of kindness, a turning point, something a grandparent told you. Picture it from the beginning, in order. Who was there? What was said? What did it change? Let the details come back slowly, like Luke gathering what the eyewitnesses said. After the sit, if you can, write it down: even five sentences, carefully, so someone you love could read it one day. If you pray, you can give thanks for that moment. If you don't, simply hold it with care. The bell holds the time.
An orderly account. Luke's promise to Theophilus: a careful, researched telling, from the eyewitnesses, set down in order.
Your line: so you may know. Today, write your five careful sentences, and if you're curious, read Luke's first four verses for yourself. Day five hundred two.

503.title: Zechariah in the temple (Luke 1:5–17)
503.hook: an old priest's prayer is answered at last in the holy place
503.howItsDone: Some churches read the story of Zechariah in the weeks before Christmas, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor Zechariah and Elizabeth as saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's cover letter to Theophilus, an orderly account. Your line was so you may know. Did you write your five careful sentences? Day five hundred three.

Luke's story doesn't open in a palace, or even in Nazareth. It opens with an elderly couple who have done everything right. In the King James Bible: "There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias." That's the Greek form of Zechariah. His wife is Elisabeth, from a priestly family too. Luke says they were both righteous, walking in all the commandments blameless. And then the line that hurts: "they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years." Good people. Faithful people. And the one thing they prayed for never came.

Zechariah's priestly division is on duty at the temple in Jerusalem. Duties go by lot, Luke says, the custom of the priest's office, and the lot falls on him to go into the temple of the Lord and burn incense. Jewish tradition later recorded that a priest might get that honor only once in his life. So here is an old man, alone at the altar of incense, smoke rising, while outside the whole crowd prays. And suddenly an angel is standing at the right side of the altar. Zechariah is terrified. And the angel's first words are these: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John." Thy prayer is heard. Which prayer? Probably the one for a child, prayed for decades, maybe given up on years ago. Some readers also hear the prayer for Israel's rescue that the priest was offering that very hour. Either way, the answer comes in the holy place. Some readers hear the names, too: in Hebrew, Zechariah is usually taken to mean the LORD has remembered, and John, God is gracious. Then the angel describes the child: he will go before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children." Those words echo the closing lines of Malachi, which we heard seven days ago: the last book of the prophets in Christian Bibles. Its final promise is picked up in the first scene of Luke, in the temple. In Luke's telling, the waiting is over. Christians hear the whole Gospel starting here: not with fanfare, but with a faithful old man whose prayer was heard.
screen: `THE LOT FALLS: INCENSE IN THE HOLY PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray again for an old prayer. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you hoped or prayed for a long time ago and quietly stopped asking about. A healing, a reconciliation, a child, a door that never opened, a change in someone you love. Don't force any feeling about it. Just take it out and look at it again, the way Zechariah might have, one more time, with the incense rising. Notice whether there's still hope in you, or tiredness, or both. If you pray, you can offer that old prayer to God again, as honestly as you can. If you don't, simply hold the hope gently for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
Zechariah in the temple. An old, faithful priest, chosen by lot to burn incense, told by an angel: fear not, thy prayer is heard.
Your line: your prayer is heard. Today, if someone tells you about something they've long hoped for, don't rush to advise. Just say: that matters. Day five hundred three.

504.title: Struck silent (Luke 1:18–25)
504.hook: he doubts and can't speak for nine months; Elizabeth hides and rejoices
504.howItsDone: Some Christians keep times of silence as a way of waiting, especially in Advent, and some monastic rules, like Saint Benedict's, make silence part of daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zechariah in the temple, an old priest alone with the incense, and an angel saying fear not. Your line was your prayer is heard. Did you take out an old hope and look at it again? Day five hundred four.

An angel has just promised Zechariah the son he and Elisabeth prayed for. And what does he say? Not thank you. Not finally. He says, in the King James Bible: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years." How can I be sure? It's such a human reply. He and his wife are well stricken in years, and after that long, hope can feel dangerous. It's an old reflex: good news arrives, and the first move is to look for the catch. But this time, the messenger is not amused. He tells Zechariah exactly who he is.

"I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings." Then the sign Zechariah asked for, though not the one he wanted: "thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed." Dumb, in older English, means unable to speak. Outside, the crowd is waiting, wondering why he's taking so long. When he finally comes out, he can't say a word to them. He just makes signs with his hands. Here's a detail worth holding onto: near the very end of Luke's Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his friends. Some readers see the Gospel opening with a blessing that couldn't be spoken, and closing with one that finally is. Zechariah goes home in silence. And then Elisabeth conceives. Luke says she hid herself five months, and she says: "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men." Reproach is her own word for the way people had looked at her. Now, she says, the Lord has looked on her. She doesn't announce it. She keeps it close, like something too precious to show yet. So the house is quiet. A man who can't speak, a woman who won't, and a child growing in the silence. Christians have read Zechariah's silence in more than one way: as a consequence of doubt, and also as a gift, months to listen instead of talk. This week has come a long way: a mother who can't forget, a balm, a scroll in Nazareth, the prophets' voices, Luke's careful letter, an old priest's prayer, and now a quiet house where something is growing.

When words start up in your head, notice them, and let them pass like Zechariah's crowd outside the door. Then think about the day ahead. Where do you usually talk too much? Filling silences in meetings, explaining yourself, giving advice nobody asked for, arguing online. Choose one of those places and decide to use fewer words there today. If you pray, you can offer your silence to God as a kind of listening. If you don't, simply rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
